# What Python is {#sec-overview .unnumbered}

Python is a general-purpose, interpreted language with dynamic types and blocks
marked by indentation. It reads close to pseudocode, and its core is small. The
work is done by libraries: NumPy for arrays, pandas and Polars for tables,
SciPy for numerics, Matplotlib for plots, scikit-learn and PyTorch for machine
learning. Most of them are compiled code in C, C++, Fortran, or Rust behind a
Python interface, so a Python program is mostly glue that reads data, calls
these libraries, and writes results.

That makes Python one of the most widely used languages of research software,
in academia and in industry, for analysis scripts, notebooks, libraries, the
steps of workflows ([](../tools/workflows/index.qmd)), and services
([](../tools/services/fastapi.qmd)). It is slow only where the work happens in
Python itself: a loop over millions of elements runs far slower than the same
operation on an array. Express such work as array operations
(@sec-arrays), and only when that is not enough, move the hot spot to compiled
code, for example with Numba, Cython, or Rust. Performance ranks below
correctness and clarity
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-quality)), so measure before optimizing.
Threads do not speed up pure Python code, because of the global interpreter
lock; parallelism comes from processes or from compiled libraries.

Working in Python comes down to a mental model (@sec-model), a small set of
syntax (@sec-syntax), and a few tools (@sec-tooling). The rules at the end
(@sec-rules) apply the principles to Python.

Checked against Python 3.12, uv 0.13, Ruff 0.17, and pytest 9.

# How Python thinks {#sec-model}

Three facts explain most of the surprises of Python in research software: a
name refers to an object and never holds a copy of it (@sec-names), types are
checked only when the code runs (@sec-types), and importing a module runs it
(@sec-modules).


## A name refers to an object {#sec-names}

Assignment binds a name to an object and never copies it. After `b = a`, there
is one object with two names, and a change made through one name shows through
the other:

```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a              # a second name for the same list, not a copy
b.append(4)
print(a)           # [1, 2, 3, 4]
c = a.copy()       # a copy: changing c leaves a alone
```

Numbers, strings, and tuples are immutable, so sharing them is harmless. Lists,
dictionaries, sets, NumPy arrays, and pandas data frames are mutable, and a
function receives the very objects its caller passed. A function that changes
its argument therefore changes the data of its caller, which is the defect that
[](../principles/design.qmd#sec-mutation) warns about. Copy first, or build a
new object and return it.

A slice of a NumPy array is a view on the same memory, not a copy, unlike a
slice of a list. Indexing with a mask or a list of indices does copy:

```python
x = np.arange(5)
y = x[:3]          # a view on x
y[0] = 99          # x[0] is now 99 as well
z = x[:3].copy()   # a copy, independent of x
```


## Types are checked when the code runs {#sec-types}

A name has no type, its object has one, and Python checks the types of the
operands only when a line runs. A wrong type therefore shows up deep inside a
long job instead of at the start. Python is duck-typed: a function works with
any object that supports the operations it uses, whether a list, a NumPy array,
or a pandas series. Type hints, such as `x: float`, document the types and let a
type checker, such as mypy or pyright, find mismatches before the code runs;
Python itself ignores them.

Two facts about numbers matter in research software. An `int` has unlimited
size, but a `float` is an IEEE 754 double, so `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `False`;
compare with `math.isclose` or `numpy.isclose`, and in tests with
`pytest.approx` ([](../principles/testing.qmd#sec-float-tests)). And `/` always
divides as floats, while `//` rounds down.


## Importing a module runs it {#sec-modules}

A file `.py` is a module, and a folder of modules with an `__init__.py` is a
package. `import` runs the top level of a module once, so code at the top level
of a module runs at import
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-import)). Put the work of a script behind a
guard, so that the file can be imported without running it:

```python
def main():
    ...

if __name__ == "__main__":   # true only when the file is run directly
    main()
```

Install your own code as a package instead of changing `sys.path`: with uv,
`uv sync` installs the project in its environment (@sec-uv), and its modules
import from anywhere.


# Essential syntax {#sec-syntax}

The following is the part of Python that most research code is made of.


## Values and collections {#sec-values}

```python
n = 3                         # int
rate = 0.05                   # float
name = "station-7"            # str
ok = True                     # bool
nothing = None                # the absence of a value

values = [2.5, 3.1, 4.0]      # list: ordered, mutable
point = (52.5, 13.4)          # tuple: ordered, immutable
ages = {"ana": 31, "bo": 28}  # dict: key to value, in insertion order
unique = {1, 2, 2, 3}         # set: {1, 2, 3}

values[0], values[-1], values[1:]   # first, last, all but the first
ages["ana"]                         # 31; a missing key raises KeyError
ages.get("cy", 0)                   # 0, the default for a missing key
f"{name} has {len(values)} values"  # an f-string
```


## Conditionals and loops {#sec-control}

```python
if rate > 0.1:
    print("high")
elif rate > 0:
    print("low")
else:
    print("zero")

for v in values:                       # over the items
    print(v)
for i, v in enumerate(values):         # with the index
    print(i, v)
for k, v in ages.items():              # over a dictionary
    print(k, v)
for a, b in zip(values, values[1:]):   # in pairs
    print(b - a)
while n > 0:                           # break and continue work as usual
    n -= 1

squares = [v**2 for v in values]                       # list comprehension
adults = {k: v for k, v in ages.items() if v >= 30}    # dict comprehension
```

In a condition, `0`, `None`, `""`, and every empty collection count as false.
A NumPy array with more than one element is neither true nor false and raises
an error; ask `.any()` or `.all()`.


## Functions {#sec-functions}

```python
def drift_rate(
    distance_m: float, days: float, *, per_year: bool = False
) -> float:
    """Mean drift rate of a station.

    Parameters
    ----------
    distance_m : float
        Distance moved, in meters.
    days : float
        Time span, in days; must be positive.
    per_year : bool, default False
        Return meters per year instead of meters per day.

    Returns
    -------
    float
        The rate, in meters per day or per year.
    """
    if days <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"days must be positive, got {days}")
    rate = distance_m / days
    return rate * 365.25 if per_year else rate

drift_rate(12.0, 30)                       # by position
drift_rate(12.0, days=30, per_year=True)   # by keyword
```

The `*` makes every parameter after it keyword-only, so a caller must name
`per_year` and cannot mix up flags. A function without `return` returns
`None`, and `return a, b` returns a tuple. The docstring is in the NumPy style;
the Google style is the other common one.


## Classes {#sec-classes}

Research code needs fewer classes than one might expect. For a record of
related values, a frozen data class is enough:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)       # frozen: assigning to a field is an error
class Station:
    name: str
    latitude: float
    longitude: float

    def label(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.name} ({self.latitude}, {self.longitude})"

s = Station("Alpha", 52.5, 13.4)
s.label()                     # 'Alpha (52.5, 13.4)'
```


## Errors {#sec-errors}

```python
try:
    rate = drift_rate(12.0, 0)
except ValueError as err:     # catch the specific error, never a bare except
    print(f"skipped: {err}")
else:
    print(rate)               # runs only if nothing was raised
finally:
    print("done")             # runs in any case
```

Raise an exception for what the caller must fix, warn with `warnings.warn` for
what the result can survive
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-output)), and catch only what you can handle.


## Files and paths {#sec-files}

```python
from pathlib import Path
import json

path = Path("data") / "stations.json"      # join paths with /, not with +
path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
with path.open("w") as f:                  # closed when the block ends
    json.dump({"a": 1}, f)
config = json.loads(path.read_text())
sorted(Path("data").glob("*.json"))        # the files that match a pattern
```


## Arrays and tables {#sec-arrays}

NumPy applies an operation to a whole array at once, in compiled code. Write
array expressions instead of loops:

```python
import numpy as np

x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0])
x * 2 + 1                       # element by element, no loop
x[x > 1.5]                      # a mask: [2., 4., 8.]
np.mean(x), np.std(x, ddof=1)   # ddof=1: the sample standard deviation
m = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
m.sum(axis=0)                   # sums over the rows: one value per column
m - m.mean(axis=0)              # broadcasting: subtract each column's mean
```

Defaults differ between the libraries, and the difference is a number that is
wrong without a warning ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-numeric-defaults)):
`np.std(x)` divides by `n`, but `pandas.Series.std()` divides by `n - 1`, and
`np.mean` of an array with a `nan` is `nan`, but pandas skips missing values
unless told not to. State the choice, as in `ddof=1`, and `skipna=False` where
a missing value must not be dropped
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-missing)).

pandas holds tables with named columns:

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("measurements.csv")          # a table
df["temp_k"] = df["temp_c"] + 273.15          # a new column
warm = df[df["temp_c"] > 20]                  # rows by a condition
df.groupby("station")["temp_c"].mean()        # the mean per station
df.merge(stations, on="station", how="left")  # join two tables
```


# Tooling {#sec-tooling}

| Job | Tool |
|-------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Python version, environment, dependencies, lock file | uv; pip and venv are the baseline; conda or pixi when packages need non-Python libraries |
| Project metadata and tool settings | `pyproject.toml` |
| Tests | pytest; Hypothesis for property-based tests |
| Lint and format | Ruff |
| Types | mypy or pyright |
| Reference documentation | docstrings, built with Sphinx or MkDocs |
| Notebooks and reports | Jupyter, Quarto |


## A project with uv {#sec-uv}

uv manages the Python version, the virtual environment, the dependencies, and
the lock file `uv.lock` in one tool:

```bash
uv init --lib stationfit    # a new package with pyproject.toml and src/
cd stationfit
uv add numpy pandas         # add dependencies, and update the lock file
uv add --dev pytest ruff    # dependencies for development only
uv sync                     # create .venv exactly as uv.lock says
uv run pytest               # run a command in the project's environment
uv lock --upgrade           # deliberately update the locked versions
```

`pyproject.toml` declares what the project needs, and `uv.lock` records the
exact versions that were resolved from it. `uv add` writes the newest version
as a lower bound; loosen it to the oldest version that works, in a library
(@sec-pyproject). Commit both files, and never `.venv/`.

```toml
[project]
name = "stationfit"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["numpy>=2.0", "pandas>=2.2"]

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["pytest", "ruff"]
```


## Test with pytest {#sec-pytest}

pytest collects the functions `test_*` in the files `test_*.py` and runs them.
A plain `assert` is enough; pytest shows the values when it fails.

```python
import pytest
from stationfit import drift_rate

def test_drift_rate_per_day():
    assert drift_rate(12.0, 30) == pytest.approx(0.4)   # relative tolerance

@pytest.mark.parametrize("days", [0, -1])               # one test per value
def test_nonpositive_days_raise(days):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        drift_rate(12.0, days)
```

```bash
uv run pytest             # all tests
uv run pytest -x          # stop at the first failure
uv run pytest -k drift    # only tests with "drift" in their name
uv run pytest --lf        # only the tests that failed last time
```

`pytest.approx` compares floats with a tolerance
([](../principles/testing.qmd#sec-float-tests)), and `pytest.raises` tests the
edges ([](../principles/testing.qmd#sec-edges)).


## Check with Ruff {#sec-ruff}

```bash
uv run ruff check           # lint
uv run ruff check --fix     # lint, and fix what can be fixed safely
uv run ruff format          # format
```

Ruff's rules are chosen in `pyproject.toml`. The rule sets `F` (pyflakes), `B`
(bugbear), and `NPY` (NumPy) find real defects, such as unused names, mutable
defaults, and removed NumPy functions:

```toml
[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "B", "NPY"]
```


# Rules {#sec-rules}


## No mutable default arguments {#sec-mutable-defaults}

A default value of a parameter must not be a mutable object, such as a list, a
dictionary, a set, or an array. Python evaluates the default once, when `def`
runs, not at each call, so all calls share one object, and whatever a call
appends to it, the next call finds:

```python
def collect(x, acc=[]):       # wrong: one list for all calls
    acc.append(x)
    return acc

collect(1)                    # [1]
collect(2)                    # [1, 2], not [2]

def collect(x, acc=None):     # right: a new list at each call
    if acc is None:
        acc = []
    acc.append(x)
    return acc
```

The function then returns different results for the same arguments, depending
on the calls before it, which is global state
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-global-state)). Ruff's rule `B006` finds it.


## Declare the dependencies, and lock them for workflow code {#sec-pyproject}

Every project should declare in `pyproject.toml` the Python version it needs
(`requires-python`) and every package it imports. A library declares the range
of versions that it works with, as its users install it next to other packages;
workflow code should in addition commit a lock file, such as `uv.lock`, which
pins the exact versions ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-pin)). The lock file
is part of the recipe of the results
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-recipe)), so keep it in the repository of the
code. A workflow that runs in a container image records the digest of the image
instead ([](../tools/containers/index.qmd#sec-record)).


## Every user-facing function has a docstring {#sec-docstrings}

A user-facing function should have a docstring in one style, NumPy or Google,
that states what the function computes, and for every parameter and the return
value its meaning, shape, unit, and default
([](../principles/documenting.qmd#sec-reference)). Tools build the reference
from the docstrings, and `help(drift_rate)` shows them, so they stay next to
the code they describe. Use type hints for the types, and spend the words of
the docstring on what the signature cannot say.
